title: The Spice Counter
blurb: Six days behind a provision shop counter. Scoop, grind and bag each blend before your customers lose patience.
fact: Not every blend goes through the mill. Panch phoron, a Bengali mix of five seeds, is usually kept whole and fried in oil before anything else goes in the pot. That's why yours never went near the mill.
credit: Inspired by A provision shop selling spices in Little India, postcard, c. 1980s, accession no. 2008-05275, collection of the National Museum of Singapore, Roots.sg. Customers, prices and scoop counts are made up for the game. Game art includes original AI-generated customer portraits and shop scenery. Background music is an original synthesized Indian-inspired instrumental.

days.title: Opening up
days.intro: Your first morning at the counter. Two blends, six sacks, and customers who'll wait a while.
steps: Tap a sack for one scoop. The order slip keeps count.
Press Grind & bag. The mill runs by itself, so start the next mix.
Tap the finished packet, then the customer it's for.

days.title: Sambar day
days.intro: Sambar powder joins the list, heavy on chilli with a little bitter fenugreek. A third customer can reach the counter now.

days.title: Keep it whole
days.intro: Panch phoron is five seeds in equal parts, and it stays whole. Skip the mill and press Bag whole. Grind it and it's ruined.

days.title: A second mill
days.intro: Meat curry powder and garam masala bring in the warm spices: cinnamon, cloves and cardamom. Two mills now, so keep both turning.

days.title: The regulars
days.intro: Regulars don't read out recipes. They just say what they want. Can't remember one? Peek at the book for $1.

days.title: Deepavali week
days.intro: The busiest week of the year. Everyone's cooking for family, and four customers can crowd the counter at once.

about.title: A provision shop in Little India

cards.title: Before it was Little India
cards.text: The district was simply called Serangoon, after one of Singapore's earliest roads. The name Little India only became official in the 1980s, around the time of this postcard.

cards.title: Shops for a growing community
cards.text: As the Indian population grew, shops sprang up to serve it: garland makers, goldsmiths, tailors, restaurateurs, and sellers of saris, spices and provisions from India. Provision-shop owners were often Tamils.

cards.title: Deepavali on Campbell Lane
cards.text: Today Campbell Lane hosts a Festival Village at Deepavali, with pushcarts selling costumes, jewellery, food, handicrafts, spices and carpets.

cards.title: Every cook's own ratio
cards.text: The scoop counts here are simplified for the game. Real blends vary by brand, region and family, and sambar powder usually has lentils and rice in it too.

sources.facts: Facts: Little India: A Cultural and Historical Precinct by Ruchi Mittal (MuseSG, June 2017) and the Little India Heritage Trail booklet, National Heritage Board.
media: Blend ingredients drawn from: Bong Eats (panch phoron), Veg Recipes of India (rasam), Padhu's Kitchen (sambar), Asia Society (garam masala), and the ingredient lists on Singapore retail fish and meat curry powders.
